question.text: A portfolio manager's fund has a return of 14%, a downside deviation of 8%, and the minimum acceptable return (MAR) is 6%. The fund's total standard deviation is 12%. What is the Sortino ratio, and how does it compare to the Sharpe ratio (assuming risk-free rate equals MAR)?

answer.text: Sortino = 0.67; it is lower than the Sharpe ratio of 1.00 because Sortino penalizes all volatility
Sortino = 1.00; it is higher than the Sharpe ratio of 0.67 because Sortino only penalizes downside volatility
Sortino = 0.67; it equals the Sharpe ratio because both use the same risk measure
Sortino = 1.75; it is higher because Sortino uses semi-variance which is always smaller than variance

explanation.text: The Logic: Per NISM Series X-A page 283, the Sortino ratio is excess portfolio return divided by semi-standard deviation (downside deviation): Sortino = (14% - 6%) / 8% = 1.00. Per page 281, the Sharpe ratio is excess portfolio return divided by portfolio standard deviation: Sharpe = (14% - 6%) / 12% = 0.67. Sortino exceeds Sharpe because downside deviation (8%) is less than total standard deviation (12%), making the Sortino denominator smaller. The Trap: Option A reverses the Sortino and Sharpe values and misattributes which ratio penalizes all volatility — Sharpe uses total standard deviation, Sortino uses only downside risk. Option C wrongly claims the two ratios share the same risk measure. Option D uses 14/8 (total return rather than excess return) to get 1.75, which is the wrong formula. Note: Sharpe penalizes total volatility while Sortino penalizes only returns below the minimum acceptable return, so Sortino is the more relevant ratio when only downside risk concerns the investor.
